title: Premature Return to Play After Concussion
author: Power Of Patients
content:
Many people want to know when they can return to play after concussion. In reality, it's a multi-step process, and everyone's recovery looks different.

We're here to talk about when players can consider playing again and what the step-by-step progression should look like. Read on to learn more.

It can be difficult to determine when it's safe to return to sports and activities after a concussion. No two injuries are alike, so determining a set timeframe is impossible.

In general, after one to three days of rest, doctors will allow patients to return to normal (non-exercise) activities that aren't too strenuous, but this is only under the care of medical professionals after an evaluation.

If someone is unable to undergo daily testing to ensure their cognitive and mental readiness, many professionals recommend a seven-day minimum period before the person returns to their activities, even if their concussion symptoms have abated.

Ideally, patients will undergo daily testing. During these tests, doctors will track the progression of the patient's cognitive abilities and processes.

As long as the patient is improving over time, it's a sign that they'll be able to return to normal activities soon. If a patient isn't progressing, it's a sign that there may be something wrong, and the patient would need to undergo further testing and potentially, treatment.

It's crucial for patients to take time off before they return to their sports again. Not doing so can be dangerous and in some cases, deadly.

Some professionals believe in "Second impact syndrome." This means that someone has returned to their sport after a concussion before they were finished healing. Having one concussion makes someone more likely to experience another one, and that second concussion can allegedly cause even more serious damage.

Researchers say that the second concussion is more likely to be deadly.

Again, the prevalence of second impact syndrome is low, so not all doctors believe that it's a legitimate concern. However, it's clear that returning to physical activity too soon after an injury is dangerous.

When someone is still recovering their cognitive abilities, they won't be as balanced, agile, or capable. Even if they don't get another head injury, they may find themselves with another bodily injury due to poor coordination or focus during a game.

This will result in more time spent in recovery and potentially even an inability to return to sports at all. Patients should take their initial recovery period seriously.

It's always important to take the return to play process slowly to avoid future injuries. The first step is rest. The patient must rest for several days before they start going back to their normal activities after a concussion. There should be no remaining concussion symptoms when the patient goes back to their sports-related activities.

Rest periods tend to last between one and three days unless the patient isn't showing improvement. In that case, further testing may be necessary.

Don't rush through the process. Take your time, and don't be afraid to stay at one stage for longer than what feels necessary. It's always better to be safe rather than sorry, and if that means taking some extra time to acclimate to activities again, so be it.

Here are the stages that on should go through after their rest period.

The first stage after the "rest" stage is the "return to normal" stage. This doesn't mean returning to physical activity. It means returning to whatever standard daily activities the patient participates in.

They can go back to work or school, do light cleaning duties, and go on walks. They should avoid lifting anything heavy or doing any strenuous workouts. If they feel the need to exercise, walking, yoga, and stretching are all good options if they don't notice any symptoms. Light aerobic exercise is appropriate.

During the next stage, the patient can begin to exercise again. They should take it easy. Avoid anything high intensity during this stage.

Longer or more intense walks are appropriate during this stage. Cycling at a slow pace is also a viable option, but stationary cycling is ideal because it's safer.

If the patient wants to resume muscle-toning exercises, they should avoid doing anything more strenuous than mat Pilates at this time. Again, it's important to keep an eye on symptoms and if they return, to cease activity.

This isn't the time to start jogging or lifting weights.

The next stage reintroduces sports-specific training. Again, this should be low-intensity training.

This can include skating, swimming, running drills, dribbling, and other no-contact activities. There should be no chance of the patient's head getting hit by a ball or another person.

Once the previous stage feels comfortable, the patient can start to increase their training intensity. They may start doing drills with other players (like passing drills). Again, all activities should be no-contact.

During this stage, patients can also begin to incorporate resistance training into their routines. They should still take it easy and stop if they begin to feel tired or dizzy.

This next stage is exciting for most people! This is when patients can return to normal game practice. This stage should ideally start after medical clearance and after a coach has assessed their abilities.

This is full-contact practice, but in the case of heavy-contact sports (like football or hockey), it's best to start with minimal contact and progress slowly.

Once the patient feels comfortable, they're able to return to their sport as normal. People are more likely to experience concussions after their first one, so it's important to be mindful while playing.

With all of that in mind, there are a few things that people should consider while they're going through this process. Recovering from a concussion isn't easy. Here's a quick breakdown of a few things you should keep in mind throughout recovery.

Often, people get so excited to move to the next stage that they're resistant to slowing down or going backward. When they realize they're not ready for their current stage, they don't want to wait. They let their egos get in the way of recovery.

It's okay, and even normal, to have to fall back or take breaks. One day you may feel ready to move to stage 4, the next you may realize you were more comfortable at stage 3. Don't be afraid to go back to a previous stage when you realize you're not ready.

It's common for people to see other people recover and think that their recovery process should look the same. Some athletes can move through their stages of recovery quickly and make it look easy. That doesn't mean that everyone can do this.

Go through recovery at your own pace. Don't worry about what other people are doing. Worry about your own recovery process and comfort level.

This one is crucial. Patients should wait for a minimum of 24 hours before recovery stages. In many cases, waiting an extra day or two is a good idea. Some concussion symptoms don't show up right away.

Patients may feel fine while doing their activities but realize the next day that they overexerted themselves. If you wait a full 24 hours, you're more likely to notice signs that something is wrong before you move to the next stage.

Waiting to return to play after concussion can be frustrating, but the recovery process is essential. If players don't take breaks before starting again, they risk severe injuries. A slow and steady recovery is a safe recovery.

Nobody knows when a sports-related concussion will happen, but there are certain steps to help individuals properly recover and return to their old selves. These steps include seeing a certified physician, getting a proper diagnosis, tracking any symptoms, and being kind to your body and mind.

All of these can be achieved with the help of Sallie® from Power of Patients.

Sallie® aims to assist individuals by being an incredibly easy-to-use and free symptom-tracking dashboard. The robust data collection approach includes many symptoms for our users to track.

By using Sallie®, individuals are taking the necessary steps for care and further prevention of Traumatic Brain Injuries. Whether or not you are involved in a sport or dealing with any type of brain injury, just know that Power of Patient’s Sallie® is made for you.

title: Raising Awareness on Concussions in Fall Sports
author: Power Of Patients
content:
September marks National Concussion Awareness Day, a critical period dedicated to shining a light on the pervasive issue of concussions, particularly as athletes embark on the fall sports season. This day, initiated by a young cheerleader who experienced the debilitating effects of a concussion, aims to educate the public and advocate for better safety measures in sports. The story behind this observance is one of resilience and determination, underscoring the urgent need for increased awareness and action.

Concussions are a type of traumatic brain injury (TBI), characterized by a temporary disruption of brain function due to a blow or jolt to the head. While often used interchangeably, the term "concussion" specifically refers to this temporary impairment, whereas TBI encompasses a broader range of brain injuries, from mild to severe. Understanding this distinction is crucial as we delve into the impact of concussions across various fall sports.

National Concussion Awareness Day was founded by Brooke Mills, a high school cheerleader who sustained a concussion during a cheerleading practice. Brooke's experience with the long-lasting effects of her injury and the challenges she faced in receiving proper treatment motivated her to raise awareness about the severity and commonality of concussions. Her advocacy efforts led to the establishment of this observance, which aims to educate athletes, coaches, parents, and healthcare providers about the risks and management of concussions.

Brooke's story is a testament to the resilience of young athletes and the importance of comprehensive concussion education. Since its inception, National Concussion Awareness Day has gained national recognition, with various organizations, schools, and sports teams participating in events and initiatives to promote concussion safety.

Impact and Reach National Concussion Awareness Day has significantly impacted the landscape of sports safety and concussion awareness. Schools and sports organizations across the country have adopted comprehensive concussion education programs. These programs often include mandatory training for coaches and athletes, emphasizing the importance of recognizing and reporting concussion symptoms.

Advocacy and Support The day also serves as a platform for advocacy, encouraging legislative efforts to improve concussion protocols and safety standards in youth sports. Brooke Mills, alongside other advocates, has worked with lawmakers to push for stronger concussion management policies, including mandatory rest periods and return-to-play guidelines.

Community Engagement National Concussion Awareness Day fosters community engagement through various activities such as awareness walks, educational workshops, and social media campaigns. These events aim to spread knowledge about concussion prevention and management, making concussion safety a communal effort.

Collaborations and Partnerships The observance has seen collaborations with numerous organizations dedicated to brain health and safety. Notably, Power of Patients® has partnered with several sports teams and educational institutions to promote concussion awareness and provide resources for proper concussion management. The organization's innovative tools, such as the virtual therapy dog Sallie™, offer continuous support and monitoring for individuals recovering from head injuries​​​.

Research and Development The data collected from these awareness efforts and educational programs contribute to ongoing research in concussion management and prevention. Organizations like Power of Patients use this data to develop better assessment tools, such as the Impact Injury Severity Score (IISS)™, which will be explored in the next part of this series​​​​​.

As National Concussion Awareness Day continues to grow, its mission remains clear: to ensure that every athlete, parent, and coach understands the risks associated with concussions and the importance of proper management. The observance has become a crucial part of the effort to create safer sports environments and protect the well-being of athletes at all levels.

Friday Night Lights – Football, particularly at the high school level, is well-known for its physicality and the high risk of concussions. The sport's inherent contact nature, involving tackles, collisions, and falls, makes it a prime candidate for head injuries.

Statistics and Stories: High school football accounts for the highest rate of concussions among all sports. According to the National Federation of State High School Associations (NFHS), football players experience 6.1 concussions per 10,000 athletic exposures. Stories like that of Jake, a high school quarterback who suffered multiple concussions over his playing career, illustrate the severe and sometimes career-ending consequences of these injuries. Jake's repeated head trauma led to chronic headaches, memory loss, and ultimately, his decision to retire from the sport.

The long-term effects of concussions in football are well-documented. Research published in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) has shown that repeated concussions can lead to chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a degenerative brain condition associated with memory loss, behavioral changes, and cognitive decline. These findings underscore the need for stringent concussion management and preventive measures in football.

US Open and Tennis Ball Injuries While tennis may not be the first sport that comes to mind when discussing concussions, the high-speed nature of the game poses significant risks. Players are vulnerable to head injuries from falls, collisions with the net or other players, and being struck by the ball.

Tennis-related concussions may not be as frequent as those in contact sports, but their occurrence is a stark reminder of the risks athletes face. The emphasis on quick reflexes and high-speed play increases the likelihood of accidental head impacts, necessitating proper concussion protocols and awareness. One example within tennis is highlighted when a young 13-year-old player was injured while at tennis camp one summer. The young player (Alex) was dutifully picking up tennis balls and another player continued to hit them. While standing up, Alex, was struck dead-center in her eye, causing momentary unconsciousness and a bloody nose. The bloody nose was the focus of the coach, not the suspicion of a head injury. Alex suffered detached vitreous, but was not diagnosed with a concussion for years. The mom was assured that baseball players get hit in the head all the time and she’ll “be fine”. Alex did not receive proper rehab, sustained many more repeated concussions and struggles with chronic impairments and eye “floaters”.

Cheerleading: An Underappreciated Risk Cheerleading, often perceived as a support activity rather than a competitive sport, involves complex stunts, tumbling, and high-flying acrobatics that pose significant risks for concussions. Despite its physically demanding nature, cheerleading does not receive the same level of attention as other contact sports regarding concussion prevention and treatment.

Case Study/Story: Sarah, a high school cheerleader, suffered a severe concussion during a routine practice. She was thrown into the air and, upon landing, collided with another teammate. The impact resulted in immediate dizziness, headache, and confusion. Unfortunately, due to the lack of awareness and protocols in place, Sarah's symptoms were initially dismissed, delaying her diagnosis and treatment. This case highlights the need for better concussion education and management in cheerleading.

Statistics reveal that cheerleading accounts for a significant proportion of sports-related concussions among female athletes. According to the American Academy of Pediatrics, cheerleading is the second leading cause of sports-related injuries for female athletes, following gymnastics. The high incidence of concussions in this sport underscores the necessity for improved safety measures and awareness.

Girls' Volleyball: Hidden Dangers Volleyball, another fall sport, involves frequent jumping, diving, and rapid directional changes, all of which increase the risk of head injuries. Despite its non-contact nature, volleyball players are susceptible to concussions from collisions with teammates, the ground, or the ball.

Example: Emily, a competitive volleyball player, experienced a concussion when she collided with a teammate while both were attempting to save a point. The force of the collision left her with a headache, nausea, and balance issues. Emily's recovery process was prolonged due to a lack of immediate recognition and appropriate management of her symptoms.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reports that volleyball is one of the top sports for concussion incidents among female athletes (NCBI). The repetitive impact on the head, whether from falling or ball contact, contributes to the significant risk. These statistics highlight the need for greater attention to concussion protocols and education in volleyball.

Short-Term and Long-Term Effects Concussions can have a wide range of effects, both immediate and long-lasting, impacting an athlete's physical, cognitive, and emotional health.

Short-term effects of concussions typically include headaches, dizziness, balance issues, and visual disturbances. These symptoms can last from a few days to several weeks, depending on the severity of the injury and the individual's response to treatment. Immediate recognition and proper management are crucial to prevent further complications and facilitate recovery.

Long-term effects of concussions, especially when they occur repeatedly, can be more severe and lasting. Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is one of the most concerning outcomes of repeated head injuries. This condition is characterized by progressive cognitive decline, mood disorders, and behavioral changes. CTE has been notably observed in former football players and athletes from other high-contact sports, highlighting the critical need for preventive measures and long-term monitoring of athletes.

Managing head injuries in fall sports like football, cheerleading, volleyball, and tennis requires a comprehensive approach encompassing recognition, evaluation, and rehabilitation. Proper post-injury management ensures player safety, reduces the risk of long-term complications, and promotes overall well-being.

Symptom Recognition

Educating players, coaches, and medical staff about the signs and symptoms of head injuries is essential for prompt identification and intervention. Common symptoms include headache, dizziness, confusion, memory problems, sensitivity to light or noise, nausea, and changes in mood or behavior. Players should be encouraged to report any unusual sensations or symptoms immediately, and coaches should be trained to recognize potential signs of head trauma during practices and games.

Medical Evaluation

Following a head injury, players should undergo thorough evaluation by qualified medical professionals to assess the severity of their condition and determine appropriate management strategies. This evaluation may include a comprehensive neurological examination, cognitive testing, imaging studies (such as CT or MRI scans), and assessment of balance and coordination. Timely diagnosis and treatment are critical for ensuring optimal outcomes and preventing further injury.

Gradual Return to Play

After a head injury, players should follow a structured return-to-play protocol under the guidance of healthcare providers. This protocol typically involves several stages, each with specific criteria for progression, to ensure players can safely resume physical activity without exacerbating their symptoms or risking recurrent injury. The initial phase may involve rest and symptom management, followed by a gradual reintroduction of light aerobic exercise, sport-specific drills, and full-contact practice. Monitoring symptoms throughout this process is essential to ensure safe and effective rehabilitation.

Power of Patients®, a leading platform in concussion and TBI management, offers a holistic approach to promoting safety in sports like football, cheerleading, volleyball, and tennis, supported by data-driven technologies to assist players recovering from head injuries.

At the core of Power of Patients® is its virtual therapy dog, Sallie™, designed to aid individuals recovering from head injuries. The Sallie™ app guides users through symptom tracking, management, and rehabilitation. Beyond symptom management, Power of Patients® provides educational materials on head injury prevention, expert guidance from medical professionals, and a wealth of resources to empower athletes and their caregivers.

By aggregating and anonymizing user data, the platform contributes valuable insights into the epidemiology, progression, and management of head injuries in these sports. Researchers and healthcare providers leverage this data to inform clinical studies, develop innovative therapies, and improve patient outcomes. Power of Patients® continues to play a pivotal role in advancing research and treatment strategies for head injuries, working towards creating a safer and more responsible environment for athletes at all levels.

Start tracking and managing your symptoms today by registering with Power of Patients® and joining the effort to enhance safety and well-being in sports.

To promote player safety in sports like football, cheerleading, volleyball, and tennis, it is essential to translate knowledge into actionable steps. Here are some practical measures to advocate for positive change:

Attend Safety Workshops and Training Programs

Participate in workshops and programs that focus on concussion recognition, safe techniques, and equipment fitting. These educational opportunities empower stakeholders with the knowledge and skills necessary to minimize head injury risks.

Advocate for Rule Changes and Policy Reform

Support initiatives aimed at reducing dangerous play and enhancing player safety. Advocate for rule changes that minimize head impacts and enforce strict penalties for infractions.

Promote Cultural Shifts and Attitude Changes

Foster a culture of safety and accountability within the sports community. Encourage a shift in focus from toughness to smart play, prioritizing player well-being over competitive success.

Engage in Community Outreach and Education

Raise awareness about head injuries in sports through community outreach and educational efforts. Organize informational sessions, distribute educational materials, and collaborate with local organizations to provide accurate information and support.

Participate in Medical Research

Support ongoing research efforts to understand and mitigate the risks of head injuries in sports. Participate in studies that investigate the long-term effects of head impacts and contribute to developing effective preventive measures.

Head injuries in many sports present a significant challenge that requires a multifaceted approach to address. By understanding the risks, implementing preventive strategies, and leveraging innovative platforms like Power of Patients®, we can enhance player safety and well-being.

National Concussion Awareness Day serves as a vital platform to advocate for increased recognition, better management, and prevention of concussions across all sports. By understanding the risks and implementing effective safety protocols, we can protect athletes from the immediate and long-term consequences of concussions. Support initiatives that raise awareness, educate coaches and players, and promote comprehensive concussion management strategies. Together, we can ensure a safer environment for all athletes, fostering a culture of safety and health in sports. Visit our website to learn more and register today.

As we move forward, it is essential to embrace innovative solutions like the Impact Injury Severity Score (IISS)™, which will be discussed in detail in Part 2. This tool has the potential to revolutionize concussion management and prevention, providing athletes with the necessary resources to stay safe and healthy. Stay tuned for a deeper exploration of how IISS™ can transform the landscape of sports safety and concussion prevention.

title: Research Studies Link Traumatic Brain Injuries and Sleep Apnea
author: Power Of Patients
content:
Among men, the rate of sleep apnea is higher and closer to 27%. Men also are more likely to suffer from moderate to severe sleep apnea than women.

Traumatic brain injuries (TBI) are also common in men, accounting for 18,500 hospitalizations yearly. The CDC estimates 1.7 million people visit the emergency room resulting from a TBI yearly. TBI is the leading cause of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) among veterans.

Is there a connection between TBI and sleep apnea?

Continue reading as we explore this issue, focusing on whether traumatic injuries and sleep apnea are linked.

Sleep apnea occurs when breathing stops and starts.  This happens over and over while someone is sleeping. This causes non-restorative sleep.  The body is not given the time to reset and instead spends the sleep time struggling to breathe. Your time spent sleeping is very important as it clears the body of poisonous build-ups that can lead to, among other things, memory-impaired disabilities.

Depiction of Sleep Apnea from Sleep Care Online

Loud snoring may indicate a serious problem. There are other symptoms to watch for because not everyone who has sleep apnea snores. A person who suffers from sleep apnea may also have extreme fatigue and irritability even after what is perceived to be a full night's sleep.

There are two types of sleep apnea: central and obstructive. Central sleep apnea is caused by problems associated with how your brain controls your breathing. Obstructive sleep apnea occurs when something causes the airway to be blocked repetitively. As the muscles of your chest work harder to unblock the airway, a patient may gasp for air or jerk as a result.  Doing this several times throughout the night leads to little sleep.

Untreated sleep apnea can lead to serious health consequences. Someone with sleep apnea may experience a higher risk of asthma, diabetes, high blood pressure, heart failure, and stroke.

A TBI happens when an outside blow alters brain function. A TBI can affect a patient's physical health, mental and emotional health, and cognitive health.

Our brain regulates our sleep.  It tells our body when it is time to sleep and puts our body to sleep so that it can rest. When a brain is injured many of these abilities can be affected, resulting in sleep disorders such as sleep apnea.

Traumatic brain injuries cause an increased risk of sleep disorders. A recent study of veterans showed that participants were 50% more likely to develop a sleep disorder if they had been diagnosed with a traumatic brain injury. The study continues by pointing out that individuals with a TBI were "significantly more likely to develop sleep apnea."

The degree of injury, according to the study, does not seem to determine the severity of the sleep disorder. A mild concussion can have the same effects as a moderate concussion as far as a sleep disorder, such as sleep apnea, is concerned.

A second study looked at close to 200,000 veterans. In the group of veterans that had a traumatic brain injury, close to 41% were more likely to develop a sleep disorder, including sleep apnea.  The data showed that it was much more likely for a patient to have a sleep disorder, if they had experienced a mild traumatic brain injury.

Sleeping disorders such as sleep apnea can worsen the symptoms of a traumatic brain injury. The symptoms of one compounding with the other, causing a slow recovery.

Individuals who suffer from a TBI may be subjected to further injury due to overall performance associated with the effects of both a TBI and sleep apnea. People with obstructive sleep apnea and a TBI may experience difficulties associated with the "same circuits and neural networks" being used in both instances. With the same structural networks being involved, it is likely that a traumatic brain injury would interrupt brain signals operating on the same paths that trigger central sleep apnea.

The brain controls our breathing during sleep.  After a TBI, the ability of the brain to do this may be influenced. This may cause breathing to stop and blood oxygen levels to drop in the form of sleep apnea.

A person with a traumatic brain injury needs the body to be in a healthy sleep cycle in order for the brain to heal. If someone with a TBI is experiencing interrupted sleep due to sleep apnea, the brain will continue to struggle and not heal.

Unfortunately, sleep apnea goes undetected in many individuals.  Undetected means untreated.

Sleep is vital to an individual's health. When sleep is interrupted, serious health concerns arise.  The most serious of which is related to the cardiovascular system.

People who suffer from sleep apnea will have excessive daytime fatigue as well as mood swings and declining cognitive abilities. A person with sleep apnea is having their sleep constantly interrupted causing their body not to rest and alleviate some of the chronic symptoms that have arisen.

These symptoms may be signs of an alarming bigger picture that includes type 2 diabetes, stroke, and heart attack.  High blood pressure can be made worse by the low oxygen levels induced by sleep apnea.  Atrial fibrillation can also be caused by obstructive sleep apnea.

Metabolic syndrome, which may include high blood sugar, low good cholesterol, and high levels of triglycerides, is also a byproduct of sleep apnea. Adult asthma, acid reflux, memory loss, and depression are all linked to sleep apnea as well. One of the most startling facts is associated with a recent study: adults with sleep apnea had a "twofold increased risk of sudden death from any cause". This is due to the overstimulation of the nervous system as your body attempts to get you to breathe again.

It is estimated that sleep disorders affect anywhere from 30-70% of those with a traumatic brain injury. This may include anything from insomnia to narcolepsy.  The research from this study did show a link between TBI and sleep apnea, among the many possible sleep disorders.

It was also noted that the type of sleep disorder could be directly related to the type of TBI, mild, closed, etc., and where the injury took place.  It is possible that mild head injuries, and concussions, may cause more noticeable sleep problems.

While a traumatic brain injury is related to sleep apnea, the opposite is true as well.  A person experiencing sleep apnea is at a greater risk for a traumatic brain injury due to the symptoms associated with the sleep disorder.

Changes in neurological functions attributed to a traumatic brain injury contribute to sleep problems and specifically sleep apnea. A recent study of veterans with TBI showed that the most common sleep disorder among the group was sleep apnea.

Further, the study showed that sleep apnea caused serious differences in a patient's ability to pay attention over a period of time and how their memory functioned.

Sallie® is an app created by Power of Patients to help caregivers and patients in the journey to recovery when dealing with a traumatic brain injury. Traumatic brain injuries can be very overwhelming and lead to chronic stress.  Whether you are dealing with the symptoms of a concussion or recovering from an event that left you unconscious, the ability to track your symptoms will allow for a better overall picture of your health.

A sleep disorder can severely impact your life.  It can also add to your disability, making it hard to recover.  The path to recovery is often difficult and should not be hindered by sleep disorders such as sleep apnea that disrupt your sleep patterns and make it difficult for your body to get what it needs.

Sallie® has a very intuitive dashboard that allows for ease of use when recording symptoms and the progression of those symptoms. If symptoms are left untreated, the detriment to a person's recovery and overall health can be significant. Diligently working to have good sleep hygiene while using an app like Sallie®, will help you to successfully navigate the road to recovery.

Also, working carefully with your doctor and monitoring your symptoms with the use of Sallie®, will allow for a better and possibly quicker recovery.  Begin this journey as soon as possible by signing up for Sallie® here.

title: Revolutionizing Traumatic Brain Injury Care: How Sallie™ Empowers Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation Providers

As Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation (PM&R) providers, you understand the unique challenges associated with managing traumatic brain injury (TBI) cases. From navigating complex symptom presentations to coordinating multidisciplinary care, your role in optimizing function and quality of life for TBI patients is crucial. However, the inherent complexities of TBI management can often present significant obstacles in your day-to-day practice.

In the realm of traumatic brain injury (TBI) management, PM&R providers encounter a landscape riddled with complexities. Unlike visible injuries where diagnostic tests and imaging provide tangible evidence, TBIs present a unique challenge—they are often referred to as "invisible injuries." These injuries occur within the intricate confines of the brain, where traditional diagnostic methods may fall short in capturing the full extent of the damage. Consequently, PM&R providers are tasked with navigating this enigmatic territory, relying heavily on patient-reported data to guide their assessment and treatment strategies.

At the heart of TBI management lies the indispensable role of patient-reported data. Yet, this reliance on patient self-reporting presents inherent limitations. TBI patients, grappling with the aftermath of neurological trauma, may struggle to accurately articulate their symptoms and experiences. Cognitive impairments, memory deficits, and communication barriers can impede their ability to provide a comprehensive account of their condition. Consequently, PM&R providers often find themselves in a precarious position, attempting to piece together fragmented information to form a cohesive understanding of the patient's clinical presentation.

Furthermore, the absence of a definitive diagnostic test for TBIs compounds the challenge for PM&R providers. Unlike other medical conditions where laboratory tests or imaging studies yield conclusive results, diagnosing TBIs relies heavily on clinical evaluation and symptom assessment. This diagnostic ambiguity underscores the importance of thorough and nuanced evaluation techniques, where PM&R providers must rely on their expertise to interpret subtle cues and identify patterns indicative of TBI pathology.

Moreover, TBI management extends beyond the confines of acute care settings, emphasizing the need for longitudinal monitoring and rehabilitation interventions. However, the dynamic nature of TBI symptoms, coupled with the lack of standardized monitoring tools, poses a significant hurdle for PM&R providers. Without a reliable mechanism to track symptom progression and treatment response over time, providers may struggle to gauge the efficacy of interventions and adjust treatment plans accordingly.

In essence, PM&R providers find themselves grappling with the challenge of navigating the intricacies of TBI management in the absence of definitive diagnostic tools and standardized monitoring mechanisms. The reliance on patient-reported data, coupled with the invisible nature of TBI, underscores the critical need for innovative solutions that empower providers with actionable insights to optimize patient care and outcomes.

title: Safely Returning to Play: Back-to-School Sports, Injuries, and the Power of Baseline Testing
author: Power Of Patients
content:
As the leaves turn and the school year begins anew, young athletes eagerly gear up for back-to-school sports. Whether it's football, soccer, basketball, or any other sport, these athletic activities offer valuable life lessons, camaraderie, and physical fitness for children and young adults. However, with the thrill of the game comes the potential for injuries, particularly head injuries. This article delves into the vital aspects of safely participating in fall sports, understanding sports head injuries, and the role of baseline testing in ensuring a safe return to play.

The Benefits of Youth Sports

Youth sports offer a multitude of benefits for children and teenagers, from fostering teamwork and discipline to promoting physical fitness and mental well-being. At Power of Patients, we believe in the incredible value that sports bring to young lives, and we're here to ensure that these experiences are as safe as they are enjoyable. In this article, we'll explore the positive aspects of youth sports, how they can be played safely, and the role Power of Patients plays in promoting this balance.

Before delving into safety measures, let's celebrate the many advantages of youth sports:

Physical Fitness: Youth sports keep kids active, helping them maintain a healthy weight and develop strong muscles and bones.

Social Skills: Team sports teach children cooperation, communication, and sportsmanship, skills that are valuable on and off the field.

Mental Well-being: Sports boost self-esteem and reduce the risk of anxiety and depression. They teach resilience and the importance of setting and achieving goals.

Life Lessons: From time management to leadership, sports provide a platform for youngsters to learn essential life skills.

Over past decades, the world of youth sports had been shadowed by significant risks, particularly concerning traumatic brain injuries (TBIs), concussions, and the ominous specter of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). These challenges had cast a chilling cloud over the enjoyment and safety of youth sports. However, amidst the growing fear and heightened awareness of these issues, a transformative shift has occurred.

The positive aspect of this heightened concern is that it sparked much-needed changes and initiatives within the sports community. Coaches, parents, and organizations began to prioritize injury prevention, leading to safer coaching techniques, better equipment, and heightened concussion awareness. The result? A remarkable reduction in sports-related injuries, especially among children and adolescents. This shift toward safer sports is not only beneficial; it's essential for the well-being of young athletes.The shift toward safer sports is yielding positive results.

“After more than a decade of increasing rates, the rate of contact sports-related TBI ED visits declined 32% from 2012 to 2018. This reduction was primarily the result of a decline in football-related SRR-TBI ED visits during 2013-2018. Decreased participation in tackle football (3) and implementation of contact limitations (4) were likely contributing factors to this decline” (National Library of Medicine 2020)

“Sports and recreational activities contribute to approximately 21 percent of all traumatic brain injuries among American children” (Stanford Medicine, American Association of Neurological Surgeons).

“There was a 39% decline in football related TBIs between 2013-2018. Football programs have also put more tackling and contact restrictions on the game. Tackling accounts for two thirds of the concussions and other TBIs among high school football players. Tackling techniques that reduce exposure to the head could reduce the risk of concussion by as much as 33%, the study found” (CNN).

To learn more about traumatic brain injuries, signs and symptoms, and more about TBIs in general, see our previous blog posts:

What Is TBI: Understanding How It Affects the Brain and Recovery Process

TBI Awareness: Your Guide to Symptoms, Causes, and Treatments

Everything You Need To Know About Different Types of Concussions

Long Term Effects of an Untreated Concussion

The Differences Between Males and Females with Brain Injuries

Brain Imaging for Sports-Related Concussions: When is it Necessary?

The 6 Stages of Concussion Recovery: Progress and Rehabilitation

Can You Get a Concussion Without Hitting Your Head? Causes and Symptoms of a Non-Head Impact Concuss

While the benefits of youth sports are undeniable, it's essential to acknowledge the inherent risks associated with athletic activities. Among these risks, sports injuries stand out as a potential threat to the well-being of young athletes. Let's take a closer look at some key aspects of sports injuries:

Understanding the types of injuries that can occur in sports is crucial for parents, coaches, and athletes themselves. While injuries can vary depending on the sport, some common types include sprains, strains, fractures, and concussions.

As we transition into the fall season, certain sports become more prominent, such as football and soccer. With these sports come the risks of fall-related injuries. It's essential to be aware of the specific safety measures needed for fall sports.

To appreciate the importance of youth sports safety, it's helpful to delve into the numbers and trends associated with sports injuries. Let's consider some thought-provoking statistics:

How Many Sports Injuries Occur Each Year: Sports and recreational activities contribute to approximately 21 percent of all traumatic brain injuries among American children. This statistic highlights the need for vigilance when it comes to youth sports safety.

Sports Concussions: Concussions have been a focal point of concern in recent years. The rate of contact sports-related traumatic brain injury emergency department visits declined by 32% from 2012 to 2018. This reduction is attributed to various factors, including decreased participation in tackle football and improved concussion awareness.

Preventing Concussions: Tackling accounts for two-thirds of concussions and other traumatic brain injuries among high school football players. Implementing tackling techniques that reduce exposure to the head could reduce the risk of concussion by as much as 33%.

These statistics underscore the importance of proactive measures to prevent sports-related injuries, particularly head injuries like concussions. As we explore further, we'll discover how a structured approach to return to play can significantly contribute to youth sports safety.

Vulnerability of Developing Brains: Children and adolescents have developing brains that are more vulnerable to the effects of concussions. Their brains are still maturing, and any injury can potentially disrupt this process.

Long-Term Consequences: Research has shown that repeated concussions, especially if not managed properly, can lead to long-term consequences, including cognitive impairment, mood disorders, and even chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

Educational Impact: Concussions can affect a student-athlete's ability to focus, concentrate, and perform well academically. Missing school due to concussion recovery can lead to academic setbacks.

Physical and Emotional Well-being: Concussions can result in physical symptoms (headaches, dizziness, fatigue) and emotional symptoms (irritability, depression, anxiety) that can impact a young athlete's overall well-being and quality of life.

Safety Concerns: Parents and guardians want their children to participate in sports safely. The increased awareness of concussions has led to a demand for safer playing conditions and better injury management protocols.

Legal and Liability Issues: Schools, sports organizations, and institutions are increasingly aware of their legal and liability responsibilities regarding player safety. Failing to address concussions appropriately can lead to legal consequences.

Media Attention: High-profile cases of concussion-related issues in professional athletes have garnered significant media attention. This has increased public awareness and concern about concussions in sports.

Preventable Nature: Many concussions are preventable with proper education, equipment, and adherence to safety guidelines. This fact has underscored the importance of taking proactive measures to reduce the incidence of concussions.

Overall, the concern about concussions in youth sports arises from the recognition that young athletes are particularly vulnerable, and proper precautions must be taken to protect their health and well-being while allowing them to enjoy the benefits of sports participation.

1. Know the Rules and Techniques: It's crucial for both parents and young athletes to understand the rules and techniques of the sport they're participating in. Proper training and adherence to rules can significantly reduce the risk of injuries.

2. Wear Appropriate Protective Gear: Depending on the sport, athletes should wear the necessary protective gear, such as helmets, mouthguards, or padding. Make sure the equipment fits correctly and is well-maintained.

3. Proper Warm-Up and Conditioning: Adequate warm-up exercises and conditioning are essential to prepare the body for physical activity and reduce the risk of strains or sprains.

4. Stay Hydrated: Dehydration can lead to fatigue and increased susceptibility to injuries. Encourage athletes to stay hydrated before, during, and after practices and games.

5. Recognize and Report Injuries: Teach young athletes the importance of recognizing injuries and reporting them promptly to coaches and parents. Ignoring pain or discomfort can lead to more severe injuries.

6. Rest and Recovery: Rest is a crucial part of any athlete's routine. Adequate sleep and recovery time between practices and games can help prevent overuse injuries and improve performance.

7. Nutrition: A well-balanced diet is essential for overall health and athletic performance. Ensure athletes are getting the nutrients they need to stay strong and energized.

8. Power of Patients Baseline Testing: Utilize the Power of Patients baseline testing, which provides valuable insights into an athlete's cognitive function when they are healthy. This baseline serves as a reference point for healthcare professionals in the event of an injury, ensuring a safer and more informed return-to-play process.

The safe play movement is gaining momentum. Organizations and movements such as the Supporting Athletes, Families and Educators to Protect the Lives of Athletic Youth SAFE PLAY Act “seek to address these concerns through best practices, support for schools, and quality research,” all of which is transforming the landscape of youth sports. Here's how:

Modern sports programs prioritize injury prevention through improved coaching techniques, rule changes, and proper equipment. Coaches and educators are continually seeking ways to create a safer sports environment.

There's now heightened awareness about concussions, leading to better diagnosis and treatment. Parents, coaches, and athletes themselves are more vigilant about recognizing concussion symptoms and ensuring appropriate care.

One significant advancement is the implementation of return-to-play protocols. Athletes are no longer rushed back into play after an injury. These protocols ensure that they are fully healed and ready to resume their favorite activities safely.

Returning to sports after a head injury requires a structured approach to ensure the athlete's safety. The CDC’s Heads Up protocol states the following: “An athlete should only move to the next step if they do not have any new symptoms at the current step. If an athlete’s symptoms come back or if he or she gets new symptoms, this is a sign that the athlete is pushing too hard. The athlete should stop these activities and the athlete’s medical provider should be contacted. After more rest and no concussion symptoms, the athlete can start at the previous step.”

In the event of an injury, especially a head injury, the return to play process plays a pivotal role in ensuring the safety of young athletes. Let's examine the key components of this process and understand how it contributes to a secure return to sports activities:

Following a concussion, a structured return to play protocol becomes essential. This protocol ensures that an athlete's cognitive function has fully recovered before they resume physical activities. It emphasizes a gradual progression through different levels of exertion.

The duration of the return to play process can vary from one athlete to another. It depends on factors such as the nature of the injury, the athlete's medical history, and their adherence to the recommended steps. While some athletes may progress quickly, others may require several weeks to complete the process.

The return to play progression is most effective when conducted as a collaborative effort involving healthcare professionals who are familiar with the athlete's physical capabilities and stamina. Athletes advance to the next level of exertion only if they are symptom-free at their current level. Any recurrence of symptoms signals the need to stop those activities and consult a medical professional.

The development of specific protocols for youth sports concussions is an essential step in ensuring the safety of young athletes. These protocols outline the procedures for recognizing and managing concussions, including the criteria for return to play.

One of the critical components of youth sports safety is baseline testing. This testing is conducted before the start of the sports season and measures various cognitive functions, including memory, attention, and reaction time. The results establish a baseline or reference point for an athlete's normal cognitive function.

In the event of a head injury, a post-injury comparison is made by conducting another assessment. This post-injury test is then compared to the baseline results to determine the extent of cognitive impairment. Such objective evaluations are vital in making informed decisions about when it's safe for an athlete to return to play.

At Power of Patients, we are committed to empowering young athletes and their families with the knowledge and tools they need to enjoy sports safely. We want every child to experience the countless benefits of sports without unnecessary risks. Our platform offers valuable resources and guidance to ensure that:

Concussion Awareness: We provide information about recognizing and responding to concussions, ensuring that no head injury goes unnoticed.

Return-to-Play Safety: Our platform emphasizes the importance of a structured approach to returning to sports activities after an injury, with safety as the top priority.

Preventive Measures: We offer insights into preventing sports-related injuries through proper education, training, and the use of appropriate protective gear.

Baseline Concussion Test Questions: Baseline testing is a critical component of managing sports head injuries.

Power of Patients® recognizes the importance of baseline testing in ensuring the safety of young athletes. Their mission extends to empowering individuals with brain injuries and providing resources for informed decision-making. By promoting the use of baseline testing in sports, Power of Patients® contributes to a safer sports environment, where athletes can enjoy the benefits of physical activity while minimizing the risks associated with head injuries.

In conclusion, as young athletes gear up for back-to-school sports, safety should always be the top priority. Parents, coaches, and athletes themselves should be aware of the importance of adhering to safety guidelines, recognizing the signs of head injuries like concussions, and utilizing baseline testing to facilitate a safe return to play. With the right knowledge and precautions, we can ensure that the fall sports season is not only enjoyable but also safe for everyone involved.

Here are the cornerstones of safe play through using baseline testing:

Preseason Neurocognitive Assessment: Before the start of the sports season, athletes undergo a baseline test that measures various cognitive functions, including memory, attention, and reaction time. This provides a baseline or reference point for the athlete's normal cognitive function.

Post-Injury Comparison: If an athlete sustains a head injury during the season, they undergo another assessment. The results of this post-injury test are compared to the baseline results to determine the extent of cognitive impairment.

Informed Return to Play: Baseline testing helps medical professionals make more informed decisions about when it's safe for an athlete to return to play. It ensures that an athlete's cognitive function has returned to its baseline level, reducing the risk of re-injury.

Objective Evaluation: Baseline testing provides an objective measure of cognitive function, helping to remove subjectivity from the return-to-play decision-making process.

Youth sports are a remarkable journey for children and teenagers, offering invaluable life lessons and experiences. While sports offer numerous benefits, safety should always be a top priority. At Power of Patients, we're passionate about making this journey not only enjoyable but also safe.

Understanding the types of sports injuries, the role of baseline testing, and the safe return-to-play protocol can help athletes and parents make informed decisions. Preventing head injuries and recognizing their dangers ensures a safer and more enjoyable sports experience for all. We believe in the power of sports to transform young lives, and we're here to ensure that every game is played smart and safe. With the right knowledge and resources, sports can continue to be a positive force in the lives of our youth.

title: Second Stroke Risk Factors: What You Need to Know
author: Power Of Patients
content:
Did you know that one in four stroke survivors are at risk of suffering from another one? This unfortunate truth can be daunting for you and your loved ones.

The good news is that there are ways to mitigate the risk of having a second stroke. That's what this article aims to cover. We've outlined all the top contributing factors that might enhance the chances of having another one.

Whether for yourself or a loved one, following these tips can help protect your long-term health and wellness. Keep reading to learn how to prevent a second stroke.

As people get older, they're more likely to have a second stroke. Statistics even show that having a stroke is uncommon for people under the age of 40. This is because as we age, our blood vessels can become weaker and more likely to get clogged.

Some common gender-related risk factors for a second stroke include hormonal changes. These can affect blood pressure and increase the risk of blood clots. Women who are pregnant or taking certain types of birth control may be at a higher risk for a second stroke.

Having certain pre-existing medical conditions can increase the risk of having a second stroke. People who have already had a stroke are also at a higher risk of having a second stroke. It's worth noting that 80% of strokes are preventable.

Certain medical procedures can also increase the risk of having a second stroke. For example, consider surgeries that involve the heart or blood vessels. These can sometimes cause small clots to form in the bloodstream, which can then travel to the brain and cause a stroke.

Additionally, some procedures involve the neck or head, such as carotid endarterectomy. These can also increase the risk of a stroke.

It's important for anyone who has had a stroke or who has any of these pre-existing medical conditions to work with a healthcare provider. This is the best way to manage their risk factors and reduce the likelihood of having a second stroke.

This may involve taking medications, for instance. It might also mean making lifestyle changes or undergoing certain medical procedures to manage underlying health conditions.

Certain lifestyle factors can also play a role in the risk of having a second stroke. Smoking, for example, can increase the risk of stroke by damaging blood vessels. Drinking alcohol in excess can also increase the risk of stroke by raising blood pressure levels.

Poor diet and lack of exercise can also increase the risk of having a second stroke. Eating foods that are high in saturated fat and cholesterol can cause plaque to build up in the blood vessels, which is of particular danger.

In contrast, consider eating a healthy diet that is rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains. Doing so can help to lower the risk of another stroke. This is of particular importance since a healthy diet can help prevent the development of diabetes. Since diabetes also increases the risk of a stroke, change your eating habits sooner rather than later.

Being physically inactive can also increase the risk of stroke. Exercise helps to strengthen the cardiovascular system and can help to lower blood pressure levels.

In addition, stress and lack of sleep can also increase the risk of stroke. They can lead to changes in blood pressure and other physiological processes.

It's up to you to do your best to prevent the possibility of an additional stroke. Tracking your possible symptoms could go a long way in helping you spot the possible signs of a second stroke and counter them. In this way, health tracking is helping us all stay on track with our wellness goals.

Certain medications can increase the risk of having a second stroke. Blood thinners, for example, are often useful to people who have had a stroke to help prevent blood clots.

However, it's essential that these medications are managed properly. Otherwise, they can increase the risk of bleeding, which can be dangerous if it occurs in the brain.

Some other medications that can increase the risk of stroke include hormonal medications. Examples would be birth control pills, which can increase the risk of blood clots.

Certain over-the-counter pain medications, such as aspirin, can also increase the risk of bleeding, too. This is particularly true if they're taken in high doses or for extended periods of time.

Anyone taking medications should work closely with their healthcare provider. Doing so is the most effective way to manage their medication regimen. Your healthcare provider is better able to monitor for any potential side effects or interactions that may increase the risk of having a second stroke.

In some cases, healthcare providers may adjust medication dosages. They might even suggest that you switch to alternative medications.

Research has shown that certain genetic factors can increase the risk of having either a first or even second stroke. For example, consider people who have a family history of high blood pressure or heart disease. They may be at a higher risk of stroke due to these factors.

In addition, certain genetic disorders can also increase the risk of stroke. For example, some people have a condition called sickle cell anemia. They have a higher risk of stroke due to changes in the structure of their blood cells.

This can also be true for people with Fabry disease or cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL). It's true that family history and genetic factors cannot be changed. Still, it's important for individuals with a family history of stroke or genetic disorders to be aware of their increased risk.

High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, is a major risk factor for having a second stroke. This is because high blood pressure can cause damage to the blood vessels in the brain. This makes them more likely to rupture or form blood clots.

Managing hypertension is possible, though, and it's an essential way to reduce the risk of having a second stroke. This can include lifestyle changes, such as eating a healthy diet, getting regular exercise, and reducing your overall stress.

In some cases, medication may also be necessary to manage high blood pressure. Remember, though, to only take medication according to the proper dosage.

Further, your healthcare provider can work. closely with you on your hypertension after you've had a first stroke. This may involve regular blood pressure monitoring, which can be of particular value. It might also mean regular check-ins with a healthcare provider and adjustments to your medication or lifestyle habits as needed.

Smoking and alcohol consumption can both increase the risk of having a second stroke. Smoking can damage blood vessels throughout the body. Heavy alcohol consumption can increase blood pressure and damage the heart muscle.

Quitting smoking and reducing alcohol consumption are crucial steps toward reducing the risk of a second stroke, though. Quitting smoking can be challenging, but there are many resources available to help. These can include nicotine replacement therapy, counseling, and support groups. Reducing alcohol consumption can also be difficult. This is especially true if you've never tried to live a completely sober life before.

The good news is that there are many strategies that can help. These can include setting limits on alcohol consumption, to start. You would also do well to avoid triggers that lead to drinking and seek support from family and friends.

Sallie® is a free health-tracking tool. It's specifically ideal for individuals who have experienced a traumatic brain injury (TBI), such as a stroke. By using Sallie®, individuals can better manage their symptoms and reduce the risk of a second stroke.

Using Sallie is simple and straightforward. Individuals can register for the tool online and start using it right away. The dashboard includes a variety of symptoms for users to track.

These include headaches, fatigue, and mood changes. Users can also add custom symptoms to track. This allows them to personalize their symptom-tracking experience.

If you or someone you know has sustained concussions or stroke-related TBIs, then you understand how overwhelming the symptoms can become. Sallie® aims to ease this feeling by being an incredibly easy-to-use and free TBI symptom-tracking dashboard.

Using the dashboard at the beginning of one’s recovery can help one to identify symptoms and triggers. The robust data collection approach includes various varying symptoms for our users to track.

If you've had a stroke, using Sallie® for your TBIs can lead to a better recovery. Register for Sallie® here.

The unfortunate truth is that brain injuries are never easy to deal with. If you or a loved one has experienced a stroke, though, tracking the symptoms through Sallie® can help. A second stroke is no joke.
